ety.text: From Latin fixus, from figō. In this modern form, it may be an early borrowing or semi-learned term; however as the one of the variant archaic past participles of the verb figgere, it may be inherited. Doublet of fitto.
Semi-learned borrowing of Latin fīxus, perfect passive participle of fīgō (“to fasten, fix”), whence also the inherited doublet hito.
Proto-Indo-European *dʰeygʷ-der. Proto-Italic *feigʷō Latin fīvō Latin fīgō Latin fīxuslbor. Portuguese fixo Learned borrowing from Latin fīxus. Doublet of the inherited fito.
From Latin castrātus.
From Latin castrātus.

From Middle English fixen, borrowed from Old French *fixer (attested only as ficher, fichier; > English fitch), from fix (“fastened; fixed”), from Latin fīxus (“immovable; steady; stable; fixed”), from fīgō (“to drive in; stick; fasten”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeygʷ- (“to jab; stick; set”). Related to dig.

senses.d: To pierce; now generally replaced by transfix.
(Of a piercing look) to direct at someone.
ex: He fixed me with a sickly grin, and said, "I told you it wouldn't work!"
She sniffed, too, comprehendingly, and fixed her son with a relentless eye.

senses.d: To attach; to affix; to hold in place or at a particular time.
ex: A dab of chewing gum will fix your note to the bulletin board.
A leech can fix itself to your skin without you feeling it.

senses.d: To focus or determine (oneself, on a concept); to fixate.
ex: She's fixed on the idea of becoming a doctor.

senses.d: To prevent enemy pawns from advancing by directly opposing the most advanced one with one of one's own pawns so as to threaten to capture any advancing backward pawns.
To mend, to repair.
ex: That heater will start a fire if you don't fix it.
You can't fix stupid.

senses.d: To be immensely pleasurable to.
ex: Some pizza rolls would fix me right now.
Getting tongued by a hot woman would fix me.

senses.d: To prepare (food or drink).
ex: She fixed dinner for the kids.

senses.d: To make (a contest, vote, or gamble) unfair; to privilege one contestant or a particular group of contestants, usually before the contest begins; to arrange immunity for defendants by tampering with the justice system via bribery or extortion.
ex: A majority of voters believed the election was fixed in favor of the incumbent.

senses.d: To surgically render an animal, especially a pet, infertile.
ex: Rover stopped digging under the fence after we had the vet fix him.

senses.d: A repair or corrective action.
ex: That plumber's fix is much better than the first one's.

senses.d: A difficult situation; a quandary or dilemma; a predicament.
ex: It rained before we repaired the roof, and were we in a fix!
"How come you're in this fix?"

senses.d: A single dose of a narcotic drug, especially when injected.
ex: And Cash told me of cases where two hips take a fix together and then one pulls out his badge.
Maybe I will find in yage what I was looking for in junk and weed and coke. Yage may be the final fix.

senses.d: Something that satisfies a yearning or a craving.
A compulsive desire or thrill.
A prearrangement of the outcome of a supposedly competitive process, such as a sporting event, a game, an election, a trial, or a bid.
ex: As the professional thief notes: You can tell by the way the case is handled in court when the fix is in.

senses.d: An understanding, grasp of something.
ex: Each character comes to us with her own particular fix on reality, shaped by a lifetime of experience and by the urgencies of the moment.

senses.d: A determination of location.
ex: We have a fix on your position.

senses.d: A non-waypoint terrain feature used to make a determination of location.
Fettlings (mixture used to line a furnace).
